title: Job 35:1–8
context: Elihu speaks again, asking whether Job claims to be more righteous than God and whether righteousness profits him. Pointing to the heavens, he argues that human sin does not harm God and human righteousness does not enrich him; their effects fall on people. This is Elihu’s argument, to be weighed alongside the prologue, where the LORD speaks with evident regard of Job’s integrity (1:8). Both traditions affirm God’s self-sufficiency as shared ground.

verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu speaks again. His speech continues without reply from Job.

Arminian readers note that Job does not answer Elihu, and the book moves next to the LORD’s speeches, so readers must weigh Elihu’s words themselves.
verses.reformedNotes:
Readers evaluate Elihu differently: as preparing for the LORD’s speeches, as a corrective, as repeating the friends’ errors, or as presumptuous.

Reformed readers hold these views variously. Both traditions read this as shared ground and declare no verdict.

verses.text: “Do you think this to be your right, or do you say, ‘My righteousness is more than God’s,’
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu asks whether Job thinks it right to claim, ‘My righteousness is more than God’s.’ Elihu frames Job’s stance sharply.

Arminian readers note that Job never says these words, so the framing is Elihu’s.
verses.reformedNotes:
Job insisted on his righteousness (27:6) but did not, in those words, claim to be more righteous than God. Whether Elihu’s framing is fair is debated.

Reformed readers weigh the charge carefully. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: that you ask, ‘What advantage will it be to you? What profit will I have, more than if I had sinned?’
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu reports Job as asking what advantage there is, and what profit he has more than if he had sinned. He cites Job’s apparent complaint.

Arminian readers see Job’s despair at the apparent pointlessness of righteousness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Job did lament that God destroys “the blameless and the wicked” (9:22), which gives Elihu’s summary some basis.

Reformed readers see the question Elihu means to answer. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: I will answer you, and your companions with you.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu says he will answer Job and his companions with him. He addresses all of them.

Arminian readers see Elihu positioning himself as answering both Job and the three friends, whom he had criticized earlier.
verses.reformedNotes:
Elihu’s anger was kindled against both Job and the friends (32:2–3).

Reformed readers see a speaker who sets himself apart from all parties. Both traditions read this as shared ground and report his claim without judging whether he succeeds.

verses.text: Look to the skies, and see. See the skies, which are higher than you.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu tells Job to look at the skies, higher than he is. Creation teaches perspective.

Arminian readers see a sound reminder of human smallness before God’s greatness, whatever one makes of Elihu’s use of it.
verses.reformedNotes:
The appeal to the heavens anticipates themes in the LORD’s speeches, which some readers see Elihu preparing for.

Reformed readers see God’s transcendence displayed in creation. Both traditions read this as shared ground about humility before the Creator.

verses.text: If you have sinned, what effect do you have against him? If your transgressions are multiplied, what do you do to him?
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu asks what effect Job’s sin has on God, and what he does to God if his transgressions multiply. God is not harmed.

Arminian readers affirm God’s independence, while noting that Scripture also speaks of God grieved by sin.
verses.reformedNotes:
Elihu’s argument stresses that God is not diminished by human sin. How this relates to Scripture’s language of God’s grief over sin is a matter of emphasis.

Reformed readers affirm God’s self-sufficiency. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: If you are righteous, what do you give him? Or what does he receive from your hand?
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu asks what Job gives God if he is righteous, or what God receives from him. God gains nothing he lacks.

Arminian readers affirm that righteousness does not place God in human debt.
verses.reformedNotes:
This is Elihu’s argument, reported, not rubber-stamped. The prologue shows God delighting in Job’s integrity (1:8), which nuances any claim that righteousness is indifferent to God.

Reformed readers affirm God’s self-sufficiency. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Your wickedness may hurt a man as you are, and your righteousness may profit a son of man.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu says wickedness can hurt a person like Job, and righteousness can profit a human being. The effects fall on people.

Arminian readers see that human conduct matters greatly for others, even if God is not diminished or enriched by it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Elihu concludes that righteousness and sin affect human beings rather than God.

Reformed readers see God’s independence and the real moral stakes of human action held together. Both traditions read this as shared ground, while weighing the argument as Elihu’s rather than the book’s final word.
